approachQuestion.prompt: A sequence contains signed integer readings, possibly repeated. Decide whether there are indices i<j<k with reading[i] < reading[k] < reading[j]. All three comparisons are strict. Return a Boolean. Example: [3,1,4,2] returns true using values 1,4,2; [1,2,2] returns false. Choose the best approach.
constraints: The input is immutable; n is between 1 and 200,000. All integers, indices, counts, and arithmetic results fit in signed 64-bit machine words; comparisons and arithmetic have unit cost.
Input and returned output are excluded from auxiliary space. Working stacks, arrays, and copies count. No hashing is used.

options.text: Scan right to left. Keep a decreasing stack and a scalar middle initially below every legal input. If the current value is smaller than middle, return true. Otherwise pop while the top is smaller than the current value, assigning each popped value to middle; then push the current value. Return false if the scan ends.
options.feedback: A popped value has a larger witness to its left in the processed suffix, so it can serve as reading[k]. Pops occur in increasing value order, and middle never decreases. Finding a still-earlier smaller value completes the strict pattern.

options.text: Use the same reverse stack method, but accept current ≤ middle and pop top ≤ current.
options.feedback: Equal values may be falsely accepted. For [1,2,2], the required strict pattern does not exist.

options.text: Return true if the global minimum occurs before the global maximum and any reading lies strictly between their values.
options.feedback: The middle-valued reading must occur after the larger witness. For [1,2,3], the extremes and intermediate value exist but the required index pattern does not.

options.text: Test the strict inequalities for every ordered index triple i<j<k.
options.feedback: It is correct but explores a cubic number of triples. The reverse scan preserves the necessary witness with shared work.

feedback.reason: Preserve a certified middle value while removing larger candidates in a reverse scan.
details: Read from the right, keeping decreasing candidates and the greatest certified middle value. A current value larger than a stack top certifies that top as a possible third member with a larger second member to its left. A later scan step with value below the certified middle completes the pattern.

Scanning from the right certifies a possible middle-sized third member only after seeing a larger second member to its left. A later smaller current value then completes the required index order. Strict inequalities must survive duplicate values.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For reverse-certified-middle, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n be the sequence length. Use one value stack and a scalar sentinel represented with a separate validity flag, so no out-of-range integer is required.
constraints: Stack push, pop, and top take amortized constant time using a growable array; each entry uses a constant number of words. Count the working stack, but exclude input and final output. No recursive call stack or hash table is used.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each value is pushed and popped once during the reverse scan.
details: Each value is scanned and pushed at most once, then popped at most once. Thus worst-case time is O(n). An increasing original sequence causes the reverse scan to retain n entries without an early success, giving O(n) auxiliary space.
